newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS: Gemina hives off industrial interests.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS: Gemina hives off industrial interests.

text.p: Italian financial holding comapny Gemina said on Friday it would hive off its industrial interests into a new company called Holding di Partecipazioni Industriali HPI Spa.
Industrial sources said the decision was a logical conclusion of Gemina's declared strategy of separating its sprawling industrial and financial interests.

Gemina said in a statement it would transfer to HPI all its direct or indirect holdings in Gemina Participations, its editorial unit RCS Editori, textile groups Fila and GFT as well as those in paper group Cartiere Burgo, Pirelli & C., SMI, and in banks Banca Commerciale Italiana, Credito Italiano, Compagnie Monegasque de Banque and the European Institute of Oncology.

It said the hiving off represented "a strategic choice of particular importance" which aimed to point up the important intrinsic value of its existing portfolio investments, and to "allow the possibility of managing those in industrial activities in contexts separate from those of a financial and merchant banking nature."

HPI would take on the role of a predominantly industrial holding company "with liquidity to carry out either further investments in holdings or to reinforce its existing portfolio stakes on national and international markets."
Gemina said a stock exchange listing would be sought for the new HPI shares but did not say when the split off would come into effect.

Gemina would manage the remaining portfolio, comprising mainly of Gemina Immobiliare, the Gemina Capital Markets group which includes Gemina Investments, Gemina Europe Bank and Banca di Credito e Commercio, as well as minority holdings in companies like the Fineurop Group.

"Thanks to its own financial and equity assets, apart from the expectations of positive results from its holdings, the Gemina group after the separation will also be able to look for investment opportunities should these arise," it said.
Following the hiving off, Gemina's net equity would fall to 230 billion lire ($150 million) from 2.305 trillion.
HPI would have net equity of 2.075 trillion lire, reserves of 731 billion lire and liquid assets of 964 billion lire at the consolidated level.
Paid up company capital would total 1.343 trillion lire, divided into 2,573.87 million ordinary shares and 112.883 million savings shares.

The company said that all existing Gemina shareholders would receive nine shares in the new company HPI for every 10 Gemina shares held. It added that holders of 1996 warrants would be entitled to subscribe to ordinary shares in Gemina and the newly created conmpany HPI until June 30, 1996.
Gemina said warrant shareholders could subscribe to shares in the two companies in the same proportion that applies to current Gemina shareholders.
The statement said newspaper and publishing group RCS, which disclosed heavy losses last year, showed continuing signs of improvement at the operating level.
The GFT textiles group was expected to show a further improvement in net results for the full year while sportswear group Fila was continuing to show rapid sales and profits growth.
Gemina returned to the black this first half, posting six months to end-June 1996 consolidated net profit of 115.1 billion lire against a 1995 first half loss of 409.2 billion.

It restated its net consolidated loss for 1995 at 678.5 billion lire. At its annual shareholders meeting in June, Gemina said it had higher charges in 1995 due to losses at Gemina Capital Markets and Gemina Financial Products.
Gemina's 1995 accounts have been the subject of scrutiny after an investigation into alleged fraudulent book-keeping was opened late last year into the company and its RCS unit.

Gemina had hit the headlines before the November raids on its offices by tax police for its planned role in an ambitious plan to merge it with agro-industrial group Ferruzzi Finanziaria, now renamed Compart, and its sister company Montedison.
